DEPARTMENT SEL LAW AND MOTION RULINGS

#9

Case Number: 23NWCV02630    Hearing Date: July 30, 2026    Dept: SEL

ZHIDONG HAO, et al. vs SG INVESTMENT LLC, et al.

CASE NO.: 23NWCV02630

HEARING: July 30, 2026 @ 9:30 a.m.

#10

TENTATIVE ORDER

Defendants SG Investment LLC, USHI, LLC, Hongpeng Wang’s Motion for Summary Judgment, or in the alternative, Summary Adjudication, as to the Second Amended Complaint is DENIED.

Defendants to give notice.

Background

This is a contractual fraud action. On August 17, 2023, Plaintiffs Zhidong Hao and Fang Wang (“Plaintiffs”) filed this action against Defendants SG Investment LLC (“SGI”), USHI, LLC (“USHI”), Hongpeng Wang (“H. Wang”), (collectively, “Defendants”) and Does 1 to 50. On November 17, 2023, Plaintiffs filed the First Amended Complaint.

On January 12, 2024, Defendants SGI and USHI filed a Cross-Complaint, alleging two causes of action for 1) Restitution under Civil Code section 1692, and 2) Unjust Enrichment.

On September 26, 2024, Plaintiffs filed the Second Amended Complaint (SAC). The SAC alleges the parties entered into an investment agreement (“Investment Agreement”), whereby Plaintiffs would invest in Defendant SG Investment LLC in exchange for shares. The SAC alleges Defendants breached the Investment Agreement, despite Plaintiffs’ full performance. The parties thereafter entered into a settlement agreement (“Settlement Agreement”), by which Defendants would make payments to resolve the underlying Investment Agreement dispute. The SAC alleges Defendants thereafter breached the Settlement Agreement. The SAC alleges the following causes of action: 1) Rescission of Settlement Agreement, 2) Breach of Settlement Agreement, 3) Breach of Contract, 4) Conversion, and 5) Unjust Enrichment.

On May 15, 2026, Defendants (including H. Wang) filed a First Amended Cross-Complaint (FACC), alleging causes of action for 1) Restitution under Civil Code section 1692, 2) Unjust Enrichment, and 3) Breach of Settlement Agreement.

On December 9, 2025, the Court heard Plaintiffs’ Motion for Summary Judgment, or in the alternative, Summary Adjudication, on the SAC. The Motion sought 1) summary judgment on the second cause of action, or 2) in the alternative, summary adjudication on the first, third, fourth, and fifth causes of action. The Court granted the Motion for Summary Judgment as to the second cause of action. (See 12/9/25 Minute Order.)

Defendants now move for summary judgment, or in alternative, summary adjudication of the SAC.

Legal Standard

The function of a motion for summary judgment or adjudication is to allow a determination as to whether an opposing party cannot show evidentiary support for a pleading or claim and to enable an order of summary dismissal without the need for trial. (Aguilar v. Atlantic Richfield Co. (2001) 25 Cal.4th 826, 843.) Code of Civil Procedure section 437c, subdivision (c) “requires the trial judge to grant summary judgment if all the evidence submitted, and ‘all inferences reasonably deducible from the evidence’ and uncontradicted by other inferences or evidence, show that there is no triable issue as to any material fact and that the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.” (Adler v. Manor Healthcare Corp. (1992) 7 Cal.App.4th 1110, 1119, internal citations omitted.) “The function of the pleadings in a motion for summary judgment is to delimit the scope of the issues; the function of the affidavits or declarations is to disclose whether there is any triable issue of fact within the issues delimited by the pleadings.” (Juge v. County of Sacramento (1993) 12 Cal.App.4th 59, 67, citing FPI Development, Inc. v. Nakashima (1991) 231 Cal.App.3d 367, 381-382.)

In moving for summary judgment, a defendant has met its “burden of showing that a cause of action has no merit if the party has shown that one or more elements of the cause of action, even if not separately pleaded, cannot be established, or that there is a complete defense to the cause of action.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 437c, subd. (p)(2).)

Once a moving party has satisfied the initial burden of proof, the burden “shifts to the opposing party to show, by responsive separate statement and admissible evidence, that triable issues of fact exist.” (Ostayan v. Serrano Reconveyance Co. (2000) 77 Cal.App.4th 1411, 1418, disapproved on other grounds by Black Sky Cap., LLC v. Cobb (2019) 7 Cal.5th 156, 165.) To establish a triable issue of material fact, the party opposing the motion must produce substantial responsive evidence. (Sangster v. Paetkau (1998) 68 Cal.App.4th 151, 166.)

Discussion

Defendants argue that, in the Court’s December 9, 2025 ruling, the Court found that 1) the Settlement Agreement had not been rescinded, and 2) the Settlement Agreement was valid and enforceable. Defendants essentially argue that, under the Settlement Agreement, Defendants H. Wang and USIH are “Released Parties” (as defined by Section 3) covered by the Covenant Not to Sue provision of Section 4. (H. Wang Decl., ¶ 3, Exh. A.) Defendants further assert that the Covenant Not to Sue provision of Section 4 bars all causes of action alleged against SGI in the SAC, except for the Breach of Settlement Agreement cause of action.

Based on these facts, Defendants seek summary adjudication of the following issues:

- Issue No. 1: All causes of action asserted against defendants USIH and H. Wang, specifically, the First Cause of Action (Rescission of Settlement Agreement), the Second Cause of Action (Breach of Settlement Agreement), the Third Cause of Action (Breach of Contract), the Fourth Cause of Action (Conversion), and Fifth Cause of Action (Unjust Enrichment), are barred in their entirety by the Covenant Not to Sue contained in Section 4 of the Settlement Agreement entered into by the parties.

- Issue No. 2: All causes of action asserted against SGI—except for the Second Cause of Action (Breach of Settlement Agreement)—are barred by the Covenant Not to Sue contained in Section 4 of the Settlement Agreement, which limits Plaintiffs’ right to sue SGI solely to enforcement of the payment schedule set forth in Article 1 of the Settlement Agreement.

(Notice, 2:11-10.)

Plaintiffs submit an opposition to Defendants’ “motion for summary judgment or, in the alternative, summary adjudication on the First Amended Cross Complaint.” (Opp., 1: 27-28.)

In reply, Defendants argue that the instant Motion is as to Plaintiffs’ SAC, not Defendants’ FACC. Because Plaintiffs’ opposition does not address the issues in the Motion, the Motion should be granted.

Initially, the Court clarifies that the instant Motion is Defendants’ Motion for Summary Judgment, or in the alternative, Summary Adjudication on issues in the SAC. Plaintiffs’ opposition addresses a motion for summary judgment as to the FACC (filed on May 15, 2026)—such motion does not exist.

The Court finds that Defendants’ Motion is procedurally improper. The Court has granted Plaintiffs’ Motion for Summary Judgment as to the second cause of action in the SAC, implying that the motion for summary adjudication as to the remaining causes of action were moot. (See 12/9/26 Minute Order.) When a court grants a motion for summary judgment, it is a determination that Plaintiff is entitled to judgment as a matter of law on all claims. (See Hypertouch, Inc. v. ValueClick, Inc. (2011) 192 Cal.App.4th 805, 834 [“A summary judgment may be granted only where it is shown that the entire ‘action’ ‘has no merit.’”], citing Code Civ. Proc., § 437c.)

Through this Motion, Defendants improperly attempt to bring up arguments regarding the SAC that should have been determined concurrently with Plaintiff’s Motion for Summary Judgment/Adjudication. Defendants did not file a cross-motion for summary judgment/adjudication. Defendants did not make these arguments in its opposition to Plaintiff’s Motion. Neither did Defendants file a timely motion for reconsideration regarding any new facts or circumstances. The Court’s December 9, 2025 ruling on Plaintiffs’ Motion for Summary Judgment is operative. To the extent that Defendants would like to modify that order, such relief may be sought through other proceedings.

The Court notes that similar arguments were raised in Defendants’ Objection to Plaintiff’s [Proposed] Judgment following the December 9, 2025 ruling. Plaintiff filed a Reply to Defendants’ Objection. At the Trial Setting Conference on February 17, 2026, the Court ordered the parties to meet and confer regarding the Proposed Judgment and the Cross-Complaint. (2/17/26 Minute Order.) Nevertheless, Defendants filed this Motion on April 10, 2026.

Accordingly, Defendants’ Motion for Summary Judgment, or in the alternative, Summary Adjudication, as to the Second Amended Complaint is denied.

The parties are ordered to meet and confer regarding the Proposed Judgment following the Court’s December 9, 2025 ruling.

Case Number: 24NWCV03323    Hearing Date: July 30, 2026    Dept: SEL

JANE BA DOE, et al. vs NORWALK-LA MIRADA UNIFIED SCHOOL DISTRICT  

CASE NO.: 24NWCV03323 

HEARING: July 30, 2026 @ 9:30 a.m. 

 

#11 

TENTATIVE ORDER 

 

Defendant Norwalk-La Mirada Unified School District’s Motion to Sever is DENIED. 

 

Defendant to give notice. 

 

Background 

 

This is a negligence action for sexual assault of a minor on school property. On September 24, 2024, Plaintiff Jane BA Doe and Jane MBG Doe, a minor, by and through her guardian ad litem Bertha Cetina (“Plaintiffs”) filed this action against Defendant Norwalk-La Mirada Unified School District ("NLMUSD”) and Does 1 to 1006. The Complaint alleges that NLMUSD negligently hired, supervised, and retained teacher Scott Waln (“Waln”), who sexually abused Plaintiffs while they were his students. Plaintiff Jane BA Doe was Waln’s student in 2016 to 2017. Plaintiff Jane MGB Doe was Waln’s student in 2021 to 2022.  

 

NLMUSD now moves to sever each Plaintiffs’ claims for purposes of trial only.  

 
Legal Standard 

 

“When parties have been joined under Section 378 or 379, the court may make such orders as may appear just to prevent any party from being embarrassed, delayed, or put to undue expense, and may order separate trials or make such other order as the interests of justice may require.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 379.5.)¿ 

 

“The court, in furtherance of convenience or to avoid prejudice, or when separate trials will be conducive to expedition and economy, may order a separate trial of any cause of action, including a cause of action asserted in a cross-complaint, or of any separate issue or of any number of causes of action or issues, preserving the right of trial by jury required by the Constitution or a statute of this state or of the United States.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 1048, subd. (b).)¿ 

 

Discussion  

 

NLMUSD argue that trial should be severed because each plaintiff has a distinct legal action involving separate issues of liability, causation, and damages. NLMUSD asserts that trying the Plaintiffs’ cases in a single trial would confuse the jury on such issues, especially even that Waln’s “alleged abuse of each Plaintiff varies in nature, location, and time, such that alleged acts of WALN’s abuse toward one Plaintiff is irrelevant to that alleged toward the other Plaintiff[].” (Mot.,. 3:2-3.) Specifically, there needs to be individualized inquiries as to 1) NLMUSD’s duties to Plaintiffs, 2) NLMUSD’s alleged notice of Plaintiffs’ abuse for purposes of ratification, and 3) the nature and extent of Waln’s abuse. NLMUSD asserts that a joint trial would cause jury confusion and prejudice to its detriment. For example, “the jury is unlikely to care what the District did or didn’t do in conjunction with each of the individual Plaintiff’s claims.” (Mot., 7:17-18.) Further, testimony of each individual Plaintiff would be “highly prejudicial given the inevitable cumulative effect of combined evidence on damages” and would risk a decision based on emotion. (Mot., 8:20-21.)  

 

In opposition, Plaintiffs assert that their claims were properly joined under Code of Civil Procedure section 378. Plaintiffs assert their claims arise from NLMUSD’s “continuing failure to hire, supervise, retain, monitor, and report a single dangerous employee at a single school.” (Opp., 5:25-26.) In other words, this case arises out of a series of NLMUSD’s misconduct. Further, common questions of law and fact exist in Plaintiffs’ cases. Specifically, the following inquiries are at issue in both cases: 1) whether NLMUSD negligently hired Waln, 2) whether NLMUSD had notice of Waln’s dangerous propensities, 3) whether NLMUSD had proper policies to supervise teachers and report incidents, and 4) whether NLMUSD had a “pattern and practice” of failing to protect its students. (See Compl., ¶¶ 31-32, 55–63, 65–69, 71-77, 98.) As to duty, courts have held that a school districts’ duty to protect its students arises from its special relationship with all of its students. Thus, the case does not center around the extent and nature of Waln’s sexual abuse as to each Plaintiff—rather, it centers around the negligence of NLMUSD in protecting its students.  

 

Plaintiffs further argue that separate trials would undermine judicial economy. Two trials would require that witnesses testify twice and that the same records be introduced twice. Additionally, there would be minimal prejudice to NLMUSD if trial is not severed because 1) key evidence is cross-admissible (i.e., evidence of Waln’s abuse and NLMUSD’s notice), and 2) the presentation of damages in a multi-plaintiff case is commonplace. Plaintiffs assert that any jury confusion may be mitigated via limiting instructions, such as CACI No. 103.  

 

In reply, NLMUSD asserts that issues of notice and its supervisory policies differ as to each Plaintiff, arguing that its “conduct and knowledge from the years before 2016 are quite dissimilar to the District’s conduct and knowledge in the five years between BA’s alleged abuse and MBG’s alleged abuse in 2021.” (Reply., 4:21-23.) NLMUSD notes that evidence that it plans to present in defense to each Plaintiffs’ claims are different. NLMUSD reiterates that a single trial would result in prejudice to it, especially given the sympathetic nature of Plaintiffs’ claims.  

 

The Court agrees with Plaintiffs. The differences in the timing and extent of Waln’s abuse in each case do not make the cases completely unrelated. The Court finds that Plaintiffs’ claims involve related issues of law and fact regarding NLMUSD’s negligent hiring of Waln, whether NLMUSD had notice of Waln’s propensities, and whether NLMUSD maintained appropriate supervision/reporting policies. The Court finds that evidence from both cases are cross-admissible and go to the core of each case.  

 

Further, the Court is aware that Plaintiffs’ cumulative testimony of their abuse creates a risk that jury will be more sympathetic, resulting in prejudice to NLMUSD. Yet the Court agrees a trial severance is inappropriate means to address such concern. Exclusion of evidence is only appropriate where its prejudicial effect (such as evoking an emotional bias) is outweighed by its probative value. (See People v. Karis (1988) 46 Cal.3d 612, 638 [“The prejudice which exclusion of evidence under Evidence Code section 352 is designed to avoid is not the prejudice or damage to a defense that naturally flows from relevant, highly probative evidence. . .The ‘prejudice’ referred to in Evidence Code section 352 applies to evidence which uniquely tends to evoke an emotional bias against the defendant as an individual and which has very little effect on the issues. In applying section 352, ‘prejudicial’ is not synonymous with ‘damaging.’”], emphasis added, citations omitted.) Here, the Court finds that Plaintiffs’ testimony of their abuse and NLMUSD’s knowledge of such abuse is highly probative, and any concerns of prejudice can be mitigated with limiting instructions to the jury. 

 

Lastly, the Court finds that a trial severance would go against interests of judicial economy. A trial severance would require duplicative testimony and introduction of evidence based on the common issues in each case. 

 

Accordingly, NLMUSD’s Motion to Sever is denied.  

Case Number: 25NWCP00408    Hearing Date: July 30, 2026    Dept: SEL

TONIE PIPER, ON BEHALF OF HERSELF AND DERIVATIVELY ON BEHALF OF LOVE BEYOND WORDS, vs DEBRA HARDING, INDIVIDUALLY AND AS DIRECTOR AND MEMBER AND OFFICER OF LOVE BEYOND WORDS LLC, OF BEYOND WORDS RESIDENTIAL CARE 

CASE NO.: 25NWCP00408

HEARING: July 30, 2026 @ 9:30 a.m. 

 

#12 

TENTATIVE ORDER 

 

Defendants’ Demurrer is SUSTAINED with 30 days leave to amend as to the second, fourth, seventh, eighth, and ninth causes of action First Amended Complaint, and is SUSTAINED without leave to amend as to the fifth and sixth causes of action.  

 

Defendant to give notice. 

 

Background 

 

This is an action for corporate involuntary dissolution. On August 18, 2025, Plaintiff Tonie Piper (on behalf of herself and derivatively on behalf of Love Beyond Words) (“Plaintiff”) filed this action against Defendants Debra Harding, (individually and as director and member and officer of Love Beyond Words LLC, of Beyond Words Residential Care LLC, of Beyond Words ARF LLC, of Mayberry's LLC, and of Good Hand Home Care), Beyond Words Residential Care, Beyond Words ARF LLC, Mayberry's LLC, Good Hand Home Care, and Does 1 to 100.  

 

On January 13, 2026, Plaintiff filed the First Amended Complaint (FAC). The FAC alleges that Plaintiff and Defendant Harding entered into an Operating Agreement as the two member/owners of Love Beyond Words (“LBW”), an adult residential facility. Beyond Words Residential Care, LLC (“BWRC”) is an adult residential facility owned and operated by Defendant Harding as sole member. Beyond Words ARF, LLC, also doing business as Love Beyond Words Residential Care II, (“BWARF”) is an adult residential facility owned and operated by Defendant Harding as sole member. Mayberry’s LLC, also doing business as Love Beyond Words Residential Care, (“Mayberry’s”) is an adult residential facility owned and operated by Defendant Harding as sole member. Good Hands Home Care (“GHHC”), also doing business as Love Beyond Words Residential Care, is an adult residential facility owned and operated by Defendant Harding as sole member. 

 

The FAC alleges that the forgoing entities (hereinafter, “LBW Alter Ego Entities”) were created by Defendant Debra Harding “to replace LBW, to withhold the business revenue due LBW, to withhold a share of LBW profits, to take the income earnings due Plaintiff Tonie, to perform the activities of LBW, to undermine the LBW ownership interest of Plaintiff Tonie, and to unlawfully dilute LBW ownership interest of [Plaintiff]. In effect [Defendant]. . . attempted to unlawfully dissolve LBW, and thereby take any earnings, assets, and ownership interests held by or owed to Plaintiff or LBW.” (FAC, ¶ 44.) Further, the Complaint alleges that an adult residential facility must be licensed by California’s Community Care Licensing (CCL) Division. The FAC alleges that “LBW possesses CCL number 198603544, but that [BWARF] inappropriately also possesses CCL number 198603544, which implies that the CCL license was inappropriately transferred to one of the LBW Alter Ego Entities, effectively dissolving LBW and Plaintiff’s interest in LBW.” (FAC, ¶ 47.) 

 

The Complaint alleges the following causes of action: 

 

  1. Appointment of a Receiver and Involuntary Dissolution (Corp. Code §17707.03, CCP §564); 

  1. Breach of Fiduciary Duty Derivative Claim (Corp. Code, §§17709); 

  1. Breach of Fiduciary Duty Direct Claim; 

  1. Self-Dealing; 

  1. Alter Ego / Piercing the Corporate Veil; 

  1. Aiding and Abetting a Breach of Fiduciary Duty; 

  1. Accounting and for Declaratory and Injunctive Relief; 

  1. Fraud By Concealment; and  

  1. Conversion. 

 

Defendants Debra Harding, Beyond Words Residential Care, Beyond Words ARF, and Mayberry’s (collectively, “Defendants”) now demur to second, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth causes of action.  

 
Legal Standard 

 

“[A] demurrer tests the legal sufficiency of the allegations in a complaint.” (Lewis v. Safeway, Inc. (2015) 235 Cal.App.4th 385, 388.) A demurrer can be used only to challenge defects that appear on the face of the pleading under attack or from matters outside the pleading that are judicially noticeable. (See Donabedian v. Mercury Ins. Co. (“Donabedian”) (2004) 116 Cal.App.4th 968, 994 [in ruling on a demurrer, a court may not consider declarations, matters not subject to judicial notice, or documents not accepted for the truth of their contents].) For purposes of ruling on a demurrer, all facts pleaded in a complaint are assumed to be true, but the reviewing court does not assume the truth of conclusions of law. (Aubry v. Tri-City Hosp. Dist. (1992) 2 Cal.4th 962, 967.)¿ 

  

Where a demurrer is sustained, leave to amend must be allowed where there is a reasonable possibility of successful amendment. (Goodman v. Kennedy¿(1976) 18 Cal.3d 335, 348.) The burden is on the plaintiff to show the court that a pleading can be amended successfully. (Id.; Lewis v. YouTube, LLC¿(2015) 244 Cal.App.4th 118, 226.) However, “[i]f there is any reasonable possibility that the plaintiff can state a good cause of action, it is error to sustain a demurrer without leave to amend.” (Youngman v. Nevada Irrigation Dist.¿(1969) 70 Cal.2d 240, 245.)¿ 

 

Meet and Confer 

 

Code of Civil Procedure section 430.41 requires that the parties meet and confer “in person, by telephone, or by video conference.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 430.41, subd. (a).) 

 

The Notice of Motion states that the parties met and conferred telephonically regarding the issues in the Demurrer. (Notice, 1:15-16.) The Court finds that the meet and confer requirement has been met.  

 

Discussion  

 

Derivative Claims 

 

“No action shall be instituted or maintained in right of any domestic or foreign limited liability company by any member of the limited liability company unless both of the following conditions exist: 2) The plaintiff alleges in the complaint with particularity the plaintiff's efforts to secure from the managers the action the plaintiff desires or the reasons for not making that effort, and alleges further that the plaintiff has either informed the limited liability company or the managers in writing of the ultimate facts of each cause of action against each defendant or delivered to the limited liability company or the managers a true copy of the complaint that the plaintiff proposes to file.” 

 

(Corp. Code, § 17709.02, subd. (a)(2).) 

 

Defendants argue that the second, fourth, sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth causes of action subject to this Demurrer are brought derivatively on behalf on LBW. Defendants argue that Plaintiff lacks standing to bring such derivative claims because the FAC contains no allegations that Plaintiff made a proper demand under Corporation Code section 17709.02, subdivision (a)(2) before filing suit. 

 

In opposition, Plaintiff argues that the demand requirement of Corporation Code section 17709.02, subdivision (a)(2) is adequately alleged, or alternatively, is excused by futility. Plaintiff further suggests that the demand requirement does not apply to closely-held corporations, citing Jara v. Suprema Meats, Inc. (“Jara”) (2004) 121 Cal.App.4th 1238. Lastly, Plaintiff asserts that any failure to comply with demand requirement for derivative claims does not completely bar the subject causes of action because they are not completely derivative claims—they are also brought directly by Plaintiff as an individual.  

 

In reply, Defendants reiterate that the FAC fails to allege that Plaintiff made a demand to Defendant Harding that comports with the Corporation Code. Despite Plaintiff’s arguments, the FAC clearly alleges the subject causes of action as derivative actions, not direct actions. Defendants argue that Plaintiff “cannot convert her derivative claims to direct claims to avoid the rigorous derivative standing requirements.” (Reply, 3:4-5.) Defendants further note that the demand requirement applies to closely held corporations, citing Nelson v. Anderson (1999) 72 Cal. App. 4th 111, 127–28. 

 

The Court initially notes that both parties’ cited authorities involve analysis of Corporations Code section 800, pertaining to requirements for shareholder derivative actions against corporations. However, the “principles governing derivative actions in the context of corporations apply to limited liability companies and limited partnerships.” (Schrage v. Schrage (2021) 69 Cal.App.5th 126, 150.) The Court finds that the Jara case did not explicitly state that the demand requirement did not apply in derivative suits regarding closely held corporations. Rather, the Jara court held that, because certain policies favoring derivative actions were not applicable in that case, the trial court erred in in dismissing a breach of fiduciary duty claim on the ground that the claim could only be asserted in a derivative action. (Jara, supra, 121 Cal.App.4th pp. 203-204.) In other words, the court held that the minority shareholder was able to initiate a direct action against the majority shareholders for breach of fiduciary duty. (Ibid.) 

 

The Court finds that the subject causes of action are brought solely as derivative claims on behalf of LBW. Each cause of action’s heading is labeled with “DERIVATIVE CLAIM” or otherwise states that the cause of action is brought “derivatively.” (See FAC, ¶¶ 123, 167, 179, 191, 205.) The Court thus finds that the Nelson case applies. Failing to comply¿with the statutory requirements for¿bringing a derivative action deprives the shareholder of standing. (See¿Nelson v. Anderson¿(1999) 72 Cal.App.4th 111, 127 [applying the principle to a hypothetical derivative action involving a corporation held by two shareholders].)  

 

Here, the Court finds that the FAC’s allegations fail to comport with Corporation Code section 17709.02, subdivision (a)(2). The FAC vaguely alleges that the parties exchanged demand letters, which was initiated by Defendant, and that any further demand would be futile because Defendant Harding “is the sole managing member of all Defendant Companies. . .engaged in the self-dealing and wrongful conduct alleged herein, and is personally involved in the wrongdoing.” (FAC, ¶ 55.) However, the “mere threat of personal liability for approving a questioned transaction by itself is insufficient to refute the disinterestedness or independence of a director. Therefore, [a] plaintiff may not bootstrap allegations of futility by pleading merely that the directors participated in the challenged transaction or that they would be reluctant to sue themselves.” (Bader v. Anderson (2009) 179 Cal.App.4th 775, 792–793, internal quotations and citations omitted.) The bottom line is that the FAC fails to adequately allege with particularity the requirements detailed in Corporation Code section 17709.02, subdivision (a)(2). 

 

Accordingly, the Demurrer is sustained to the second, fourth, sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth causes of action with 30 days leave to amend. 

 

Fifth Cause of Action – Alter Ego/Piercing the Veil  

 

As to the fifth cause of action for alter ego/piercing the veil, Defendants argue that such claim is not recognized as an independent cause of action.  

 

In opposition, Plaintiff states that “Plaintiff does not oppose sustaining the demurrer to the Fifth Cause of Action to the exten[t] it is construed as asserting alter ego as a standalone claim.” (Opp., 10:1-2.)  

 

The Court agrees with Defendants. “A claim against a defendant, based on the alter ego theory, is not itself a claim for substantive relief. . .but rather, procedural, i.e., to disregard the corporate entity as a distinct defendant and to hold the alter ego individuals liable on the obligations of the corporation where the corporate form is being used by the individuals to escape personal liability, sanction a fraud, or promote¿injustice.” (Hennessey’s Tavern, Inc. v. American Air Filter Co.¿(1988) 204 Cal.App.3d 1351, 1359.)¿ 

 

Accordingly, the Demurrer to the fifth cause of action is sustained without leave to amend.  

 

Sixth Cause of Action – Aiding and Abetting 

 

Liability for¿aiding¿and abetting another’s tort may be imposed upon a party where that party “(a) knows the other’s conduct constitutes a breach of duty and gives substantial assistance or encouragement to the other to so act or (b) gives substantial assistance to the other in accomplishing a tortious result and the person’s own conduct, separately considered, constitutes a breach of duty to the third person.” (Casey v. U.S. Bank National Association¿(2005) 127 Cal.App.4th 1138, 1144.)  

 

Defendants argue that the sixth cause of action for aiding and abetting breach of fiduciary duty against Defendant Harding is duplicative and not actionable because Ms. Harding cannot aid and abet herself in breaching any fiduciary duty.  

 

In opposition, Plaintiff does not oppose sustaining the demurrer to the sixth cause of action to the extent that it is alleged against Defendant Harding individually. Plaintiff states that the claim “remains as to other persons or entities that knowingly participated in or benefitted from the misconduct.” (Opp., 15:13-14.) 

 

The Court finds that the aiding and abetting claim is inappropriate to the extent it alleges that Defendant Harding aided and abetted her own breach of fiduciary duties.  

 

Accordingly, the Demurrer to the sixth cause of action is sustained without leave to amend.  

 

Eighth Cause of Action – Fraudulent Concealment  

 

The elements for fraudulent concealment are as follows: 1) defendant concealed or suppressed a material fact, 2) defendant was under a duty to disclose the fact to the plaintiff, 3) defendant intentionally concealed or suppressed the fact with the intent to defraud the plaintiff, 4) plaintiff was unaware of the fact and would not have acted in the same way knowing of the concealed or suppressed fact, 5) causation, and the plaintiff sustained damage. (See Blickman Turkus, LP v. MF Downtown Sunnyvale, LLC (2008) 162 Cal.App.4th 858, 868; see also Lovejoy v. AT&T Corp. (2001) 92 Cal.App.4th 85, 96; Hahn v. Mirda (2007) 147 Cal.App.4th 740, 748.) The rule of specifically pleading how, when, where, to whom, and by what means, misrepresentations were communicated, applies to affirmative misrepresentations, not to concealment. (See Alfaro v. Community Housing Improvement System & Planning Assn., Inc. (2009) 171 Cal.App.4th 1356, 1384.)  

 

The eighth cause of action is based on Defendant Harding’s alleged fraudulent concealment regarding an unauthorized withdrawal of $150,000 from a financial account owned by LBW on April 4, 2025. (FAC, ¶¶ 194.)  

 

As to the eighth cause of action for fraudulent concealment, Defendants argue that the FAC fails to adequately state a claim. Specifically, the FAC fails to allege that any of the Defendants “(i) concealed the withdrawal of funds from LBW’s bank account; (ii) had a duty to disclose or obtain preapproval of withdrawals from the bank account; (iii) had intent to defraud LBW or Plaintiff; and (iv) engaged in any concealment which induced action or inaction by Plaintiff or LBW resulting in damage.” (Dem., 2:4-7.) Defendants assert that the FAC is contradictory. For example, the FAC alleges that had access to the same Chase Business Account in May 2025 when Plaintiff withdrew an “equal amount” of money and deposited it into an attorney-client trust account. (FAC, ¶ 85.) Further, it is unclear why Defendant Harding had a duty to disclose the withdrawal to Plaintiff where the FAC admits that Defendant Harding was solely responsible for managing the financial affairs of LBW. (FAC, ¶¶ 87, 193.)  

 

Additionally, Defendants argue that the fraudulent concealment claim fails to make any specific allegations against the remaining Defendants such that they should be implicated.  

 

In opposition, Plaintiff argues that the fraudulent concealment claim is adequately alleged. Defendants’ arguments regarding 1) Plaintiff’s access to the account or 2) whether the withdrawal was authorized are factual in nature and cannot be resolved on Demurrer. As to the lack of allegations against the remaining Defendants, Plaintiff suggests that they are implicated via the FAC’s alter ego liability theory.  

 

In reply, Defendants assert that the alter ego theory is inapplicable where the FAC alleges that Defendant Harding, not the corporate Defendants, committed the fraudulent concealment. Alter ego theory arises where a corporation’s owner abuse of the corporate form would prevent a party from recovering. In other words, alter ego liability makes an owner liable for corporate fraud, not the other way around.  

 

The Court initially addresses the alter ego theory arguments. The corporate veil may be pierced “where an abuse of the corporate privilege justifies holding the equitable ownership of a corporation liable for the actions of the corporation.” (Sonora Diamond Corp. v Superior Court¿(2000) 83 Cal.App.4th 523, 538, emphasis added.) “Under the alter ego¿doctrine. . .when the corporate form is used to. . .accomplish some [] wrongful or inequitable purpose, the courts will ignore the corporate entity and deem the corporation’s acts to be those of the persons or organizations actually controlling the corporation, in most instances the equitable owners.” (Id.) Therefore, the Court finds that the alter ego allegations cannot make the remaining Defendants liable for the actions of Defendant Harding as an individual. 

 

Further, the Court agrees with Defendants that the FAC is contradictory. The FAC alleges that Defendant Harding has exclusive control of the account and financial records, but also states that she had a duty to disclose the withdrawal to Plaintiff. For example, the FAC alleges that Defendant Harding “exercised exclusive and unilateral control over at least one LBW financial account, including the authority to withdraw, transfer, and disburse LBW funds without contemporaneous oversight.” (FAC, ¶ 193.) The Court finds that it is contradictory that Defendant Harding has a duty to disclose such withdrawal where Harding had authority to withdraw funds “without contemporaneous oversight.” (Ibid.) Additionally, the FAC fails to explicitly allege that Plaintiff would not have acted in the same way knowing of the concealed or suppressed fact. Lastly, the Court agrees with Defendants that the FAC fails to allege damages that resulted from the concealment, distinct from the damages that resulted from the withdrawal.  

 

Accordingly, the Demurrer to the eighth cause of action is sustained with 30 days leave to amend.  

 

Ninth Cause of Action – Conversion 

 

“Conversion¿is the wrongful exercise of dominion over the property of another. The elements of a¿conversion¿claim are: (1) the plaintiff’s ownership or right to possession of the property; (2) the defendant’s¿conversion¿by a wrongful act or disposition of property rights; and (3) damages.” (Lee v. Hanley¿(2015) 61 Cal.4th 1225, 1240.) ¿“Money may be the subject of conversion if the claim involves a specific, identifiable sum […].” (Welco¿Electronics, Inc. v. Mora¿(2014) 223 Cal.App.4th 202, 209.)¿ 

 

The ninth cause of action is based on the following allegation:  

 

“206. At all relevant times, LBW owned and had the immediate right to possession of its funds, financial accounts, revenues, tangible property, and intangible assets, including but not limited to cash held in LBW bank and financial accounts. 

 

207. Defendant Debra Harding was a member and managing member of LBW and exercised exclusive and unilateral control over LBW’s financial accounts and assets, including the authority to initiate withdrawals, transfers, and payments.  

 

208. Without authorization from LBW, without member approval, and without any legitimate business purpose, Defendant Debra Harding wrongfully took, withdrew, transferred, and appropriated LBW funds and assets, including but not limited to substantial sums of money withdrawn from LBW financial accounts.  

 

209. Defendant Debra Harding siphoned LBW funds and assets for:  

a. Her personal use and benefit; and  

b. The use and benefit of alter-ego corporations and entities that were owned and controlled solely by Defendant Debra Harding, and that provided no fair consideration or value to LBW in exchange. 

 

210. Defendant Debra Harding’s acts constituted the wrongful exercise of dominion and control over specifically identifiable LBW funds and property, in a manner inconsistent with LBW’s rights of ownership and possession.  

 

211. Defendant Debra Harding’s conversion was intentional, willful, and carried out with knowledge that the funds and assets belonged to LBW and not to Defendant Debra Harding personally.” 

 

(FAC, ¶¶ 208-211.)  

 

As to the ninth cause of action for conversion, Defendants argue that the FAC fails to state a cause of action. Specifically, there are no allegations that Defendant Harding lacked authority to withdraw funds from LBW’s account to manage the affairs of the company. Additionally, Defendants argue that conversion claim fails to make any specific allegations against the remaining Defendants such that they should be implicated.  

 

In opposition, Plaintiff argues that the issue of whether Defendant Harding had the authority to withdraw the funds is an issue of fact. Further, Plaintiff makes the same alter ego theory arguments in regard to the viability of conversion claim against the remaining Defendants as Plaintiff did in support of the fraudulent concealment claim.  

 

The Court initially rejects Plaintiff’s alter ego arguments for the same reasons stated in the previous section. The Court thus sustains the cause of action on these grounds.  

 

The Court finds that the conversion claim properly alleges 1) LBW’s ownership over the property, 2) Defendant Harding’s conversion based on wrongful use of the property, and 3) LBW’s damages. However, the Court notes that the conversion claim is not based on an identifiable sum of money. (See PCO, Inc. v. Christensen, Miller, Fink, Jacobs, Glaser, Weil & Shapiro, LLP¿(2007) 150 Cal.App.4th 384, 395 [“A ‘generalized claim for money [is] not actionable as conversion.’”], quoting¿Vu v. California Commerce Club, Inc.¿(1997) 58 Cal.App.4th 229, 235.) The Court thus sustained the cause of action on these separate grounds.  

 

Accordingly, the Demurrer to the ninth cause of action is sustained with 30 days leave to amend.  

 

 

 

 

 

Case Number: 26NWCV00436    Hearing Date: July 30, 2026    Dept: SEL

LLOYD A. STEVENS vs CITY OF ARTESIA, et al  

CASE NO.: 26NWCV00436 

HEARING: July 30, 2026 @ 9:30 a.m. 

 

#13 

TENTATIVE ORDER 

 

Defendants City of Artesia and Melissa Hamilton’s Demurrer to the Complaint is SUSTAINED without leave to amend.  

 

Defendants’ Motion to Strike is MOOT.  

 

Defendants to give notice. 

 

Background 

 

This is an action for injunctive relief. On February 5, 2026, Plaintiff Lloyd A. Stevens (“Plaintiff”) filed this action against Defendants City of Artesia, Melissa Hamilton, (collectively, “Defendants”) and Does 1 to 100. The Complaint alleges that Plaintiff owns two adjacent commercial properties located at 17215 Corby Avenue and 17221 Corby Avenue, Artesia, California (“Subject Properties”). On January 10, 2013, Defendants inspected the Subject Properties and determined that they were “occupied, not vacant, and compliant with applicable zoning and municipal regulations.” (Compl., ¶ 8.) Despite there being no material change in the use of the Subject Properties since that inspection, beginning in January 2026, Defendants issued multiple administrative citations under Artesia Municipal Code § 5-24.060, asserting that the properties were “vacant.” The Complaint seeks to enjoin Defendants from collecting and escalating administrative penalties prior to adjudication. The Complaint alleges two causes of action for 1) Injunctive Relief, and 2) Declaratory Relief.  

 

On February 10, 2026, the Court denied Plaintiff’s Ex Parte Application for Temporary Restraining Order and Order to Show Cause Re: Preliminary Injunction (“Ex Parte Application”). (2/10/26 Minute Order.) 

 

Defendants now demur to the Complaint.  

 

No opposition has been filed as of July 29, 2026.  

 

Requests for Judicial Notice  

 

The Court grants Defendants’ Requests for Judicial Notice of the following documents: 

 

  • Ordinance No. 25-966 passed, approved, and adopted by the City Council of the City of Artesia, California on April 14, 2025 (Exhibit E) 

  • City of Artesia Municipal Code (“AMC”), Title 5 Public Welfare, Chapter 24 Vacant Properties, sections 5-24.010 Purpose; 5-24.060 Registration and Exemptions; 5-24.070 Registration Procedure; 5-24.080 Notice; 5-24.090 Maintenance Requirements for Vacant Properties; Inspections; 5-24.110 Fees; and 5-24.120 Enforcement (Exhibit F) 

 
Legal Standard 

 

“[A] demurrer tests the legal sufficiency of the allegations in a complaint.” (Lewis v. Safeway, Inc. (2015) 235 Cal.App.4th 385, 388.) A demurrer can be used only to challenge defects that appear on the face of the pleading under attack or from matters outside the pleading that are judicially noticeable. (See Donabedian v. Mercury Ins. Co. (“Donabedian”) (2004) 116 Cal.App.4th 968, 994 [in ruling on a demurrer, a court may not consider declarations, matters not subject to judicial notice, or documents not accepted for the truth of their contents].) For purposes of ruling on a demurrer, all facts pleaded in a complaint are assumed to be true, but the reviewing court does not assume the truth of conclusions of law. (Aubry v. Tri-City Hosp. Dist. (1992) 2 Cal.4th 962, 967.)¿ 

  

Where a demurrer is sustained, leave to amend must be allowed where there is a reasonable possibility of successful amendment. (Goodman v. Kennedy¿(1976) 18 Cal.3d 335, 348.) The burden is on the plaintiff to show the court that a pleading can be amended successfully. (Id.; Lewis v. YouTube, LLC¿(2015) 244 Cal.App.4th 118, 226.) However, “[i]f there is any reasonable possibility that the plaintiff can state a good cause of action, it is error to sustain a demurrer without leave to amend.” (Youngman v. Nevada Irrigation Dist.¿(1969) 70 Cal.2d 240, 245.)¿ 

 

Meet and Confer 

 

Code of Civil Procedure section 430.41, subdivision (a) and section 435.5 require¿that the parties meet and confer¿“in person,¿by telephone, or by video conference.”¿ 

 

On February 24, 2026, Defense counsel called Plaintiff and left voicemail in an attempt to meet and confer regarding this Demurrer and Motion to Strike. (Chandler Decl., ¶ 8.) Defense counsel also sent a meet and confer letter via email and by USPS regular and certified, return-receipt mail. (Chandler Decl., ¶ 8, Exh. B.) That day, Defense counsel was contacted by attorney Boyd F. Jensen II by telephone, who identified himself as Plaintiff’s friend who previously worked with Plaintiff and his father (deceased). (Chandler Decl., ¶ 13.) Defense counsel offered a 10-day stay on the proceedings to allow Mr. Jensen time to determine if he could represent Plaintiff, but Mr. Jensen responded that he was not able to get in contact with Plaintiff. (Ibid.) As of the date the Demurrer and Motion to Strike was filed on February 27, 2026, Plaintiff has not replied to Defendants’ meet and confer efforts. (Chandler Decl., ¶ 14.)  

 

The Court finds that the parties did not meet and confer “in person,¿by telephone, or by video conference.”¿Nevertheless, the Court will address the merits of the Demurrer and Motion to Strike in interests of judicial efficiency.  

 

Discussion  

 

Defendants demur the first and second causes of action in the Complaint.  

 

“The elements of a cause of action for¿injunctive relief are (1) a tort or other wrongful act constituting a cause of action; and (2) irreparable¿injury, i.e., a factual showing that the wrongful act constitutes an actual or threatened¿injury to property or personal rights which cannot be compensated by an ordinary damage award.” (Brownfield v. Daniel Freeman Marina Hospital¿(1989) 208 Cal.App.3d 405, 410, citation omitted.) Notably, “injunctive relief is a remedy and not, in itself, a cause of action, and a cause of action must exist before¿injunctive relief can be granted.” (Camp v. Board of Supervisors¿(“Camp”) (1981) 123 Cal.App.3d 334, 356.)¿ 

 

“To qualify for¿declaratory relief, a party would have to demonstrate its action presented two essential elements: (1) a proper subject of¿declaratory relief, and (2) an actual controversy involving justiciable questions relating to the party’s rights or obligations.” (Jolley v. Chase¿Home Finance, LLC¿(2013) 213 Cal.App.4th 872, 909, quotation marks and brackets omitted.)¿ 

¿ 

A cause of action for¿declaratory relief should not be used as a second cause of action for the determination of identical issues raised in another cause of action. (General of America Insurance Co. v. Lilly¿(1968) 258 Cal.App.2d 465, 470.) “The availability of another form of relief that is adequate will usually justify refusal to grant¿declaratory relief.” (California Insurance Guarantee Association v. Superior Court¿(1991) 231 Cal.App.3d 1617, 1624.) Further, “there is no basis for¿declaratory relief where only past wrongs are involved.” (Osseous Technologies of America, Inc. v.¿DiscoveryOrtho¿Partners LLC¿(2010) 191 Cal.App.4th 357, 366, quotation marks omitted.)¿ 

 

Defendants first provide the following context to this action: On April 14, 2025, Defendant City of Artesia (hereinafter, “the City”) adopted Ordinance No. 25-966, which declares that “that vacant properties are a cause and source of blight in both residential and non-residential neighborhoods” in the City, and that properties “that remain vacant and unoccupied for any appreciable period of time become a life-safety hazard, fire hazard and attract crime (frequently involving illegal drug-related activity).” (RJN, Exh. E.) 

 

Defendants assert that the Complaint fails to state a cause of action and is uncertain. Specifically, Plaintiff cannot allege 1) irreparable harm required for the injunctive relief cause of action, and 2) the unavailability of other adequate remedies required for the declaratory relief cause of action. Defendants primarily rely on the Court’s February 10, 2026 denial of Plaintiff’s Ex Parte Application, and Plaintiff’s evidence offered in support of that Ex Parte. (2/10/26 Minute Order.) 

 

No opposition has been filed.  

 

Firstly, the Court takes judicial notice of the exhibits offered in support of Plaintiff’s Ex Parte Application. Exhibits A to D are the purported citations issued to Plaintiff by Defendant City of Artesia. Exhibit E is a “Request for Hearing Form.” All Exhibits state that, if Plaintiff wants to contest a citation, Plaintiff has 21 days to a request a hearing from the date of the citation. All Exhibits state that Plaintiff must pay all citations prior to requesting a hearing. All Exhibits allude to a “Hardship Waiver” that the recipient may submit in lieu of paying a citation. Exhibit E further states that a hearing may occur up to 60 days after the request is filed or after an advance Hardship Waiver is issued.  

 

The Court’s February 10, 2026 ruling on Plaintiff’s Ex Parte Application, states the following, in relevant part: 

 

“The Court initially acknowledges that injunctions may be issued to prevent enforcement of unconstitutional statutes, or valid statutes sought to be enforced illegally, where their enforcement would cause irreparable injury. (See Novar Corp. v. Bureau of Collection & Investigative Services (1984) 160 Cal.App.3d 1, 5-6.) However, where an administrative remedy is provided by the statute in question, that remedy usually must be exhausted before any judicial relief is sought—even where the statute is challenged on constitutional grounds. (See Board of Police Commissioners v. Superior Court (1985) 168 Cal.App.3d 420, 431-432.)  

 

Here, the Court finds that Plaintiff has not exhausted his administrative remedies prior to filing this lawsuit and ex parte application. Per the citation, if Plaintiff wishes to contest the citation, he must first do so through an administrative hearing. As noted by Defendant, if Plaintiff disagrees with the decision, he may file a Notice of Appeal with the Superior Court. Plaintiff has otherwise not shown why any exception should apply that would excuse the exhaustion of administrative remedies requirement.  

 

Further, the Court is not persuaded that the requirement to pay citation fines prior to a requesting an administrative hearing would cause Plaintiff irreparable harm considering 1) the funds may be refunded upon a favorable decision to Plaintiff at the hearing, and 2) appeal is available.” 

 

(2/10/26 Minute Order.) 

 

The Court finds that, based on the foregoing, Plaintiff cannot maintain causes of action for injunctive relief or declaratory relief where there are no allegations that Plaintiff exhausted his administrative remedies. As to the injunctive relief cause of action, the Complaint’s allegation that “Plaintiff has no adequate remedy at law” (Compl., ¶ 16) is belied by Plaintiff’s evidence offered in support of the Ex Parte Application. As to the declaratory relief cause of action, the purported live controversy—the issue of whether the Subject Properties are “vacant” within the meaning of AMC § 5-24.060—is properly adjudicated by the administrative agency first before Plaintiff may seek judicial review.  

 

As no opposition has been filed, the Court finds that Plaintiff has failed to meet his burden in showing that the Complaint can be amended to fix such deficiencies.  

 

Accordingly, Defendants’ Demurrer to the Complaint is sustained without leave to amend.  

 

Motion to Strike  

 

As the Demurrer was sustained without leave to amend, the Motion to Strike is moot.
